settings.s7: What is a managed IT services provider (MSP)?
settings.s8: An MSP is an outsourced IT partner that proactively monitors, manages and secures your business technology. That covers IT support, cloud services, cyber security and disaster recovery, without the need for a full in-house IT team.
settings.s9: Why use an MSP instead of an in-house IT team?
settings.s10: For a similar budget to a single hire, an MSP gives you a whole team with a broad skill set, proactive monitoring and expert cyber security, all for a fixed monthly cost that scales with your business.
settings.s11: What types of businesses benefit from managed IT?
settings.s12: Any business that relies on technology. We support professional services, hospitality, healthcare, construction and more, keeping systems secure, compliant and productive.
settings.s13: How much does managed IT support cost?

settings.s1: What shapes cloud projects for London businesses
settings.s2: Cloud migrations for London businesses tend to be constrained less by the technology than by the building, the lease and the calendar. The pattern repeats often enough to plan around.
settings.s4: Serviced offices remove control of the connection
settings.s5: In multi-tenant and serviced buildings you rarely control the incoming line, the contention ratio or the risers. That argues for cloud-first services, cellular failover and a design that does not assume the landlord’s network behaves.
settings.s7: Lease events are the real migration deadline
settings.s8: A move or a lease break is usually what forces the decision, which compresses the timeline and makes sequencing matter. Migrating before the move, rather than during it, avoids doing two difficult things in the same week.
settings.s10: Hybrid working is the default, not the exception
settings.s11: London teams split the week between office, home and client sites more than most. That pushes identity, conditional access and device management to the front of the design rather than treating them as a later phase.

settings.s1: Small configuration decisions can have long-term consequences
settings.s2: Technology settings are often changed little by little as businesses evolve. A new employee needs additional access, a cloud service is introduced, security policies are adjusted or a supplier makes changes during a project. Individually these updates seem minor, but over time they can leave systems configured in ways that no longer reflect how the business operates.
settings.s3: Configuration issues rarely appear after a single change. More often, they develop after years of updates made by different IT providers, software vendors and internal teams. Everything continues working, yet the organisation is carrying unnecessary operational and cyber security risk without realising it.
settings.s4: Reviews examine how your systems are actually configured against how they were intended to be, and the output is a prioritised remediation list rather than a raw scan dump. Across 2025 our average first response time was 9 minutes and our average resolution time was 6 hours, measured across every ticket we handled.

settings.s1: Most exposed passwords were never stolen from you
settings.s2: The credentials that put a business at risk usually leak somewhere else entirely. A member of staff signs up to a supplier portal, a forum or a retail site with their work email address and a password they also use at work. That third party is breached, and the pair ends up in a list traded between criminals. Nothing was compromised on your network, and nothing on your network can tell you it happened.
settings.s4: Breach dumps, combolists and stealer logs
settings.s5: Older breach dumps are the least urgent, because the password has often been changed and the hash may be slow to crack. Combolists are aggregated email and password pairs assembled for credential stuffing, which is why password reuse is the whole problem. The one that deserves immediate attention is an infostealer log, taken from a machine infected with malware that harvested everything the browser had saved along with active session cookies. Those cookies can let someone resume a signed-in session without ever needing the password or the second factor.
settings.s7: A match is not the same as a breach
settings.s8: An alert tells you a credential appeared in a dataset, not that anyone has used it. The triage questions are whether the password is still current, whether that account has multi-factor authentication, whether the same password protects anything else, and whether the source suggests a compromised device rather than a third-party leak. Answering those turns a frightening notification into a short, specific job. Treating every match as an emergency is how teams start ignoring the alerts.
settings.s10: Why monitoring is detection, not prevention
settings.s11: We would rather be straight about this. Monitoring cannot remove your data from anywhere, and no supplier can, whatever they imply. What it buys you is time between the exposure and someone trying it, which is the window in which a reset costs you ten minutes instead of an incident. It works because it sits alongside the controls that actually block the attempt: multi-factor authentication, a password manager so reuse stops being tempting, and conditional access rules that make an unexpected sign-in harder to complete.

Where the source looks like an infostealer log, the device itself is treated as compromised and taken out of use until it has been rebuilt, because rotating a password on an infected machine simply hands over the new one.

settings.s12: Trusted services
settings.s18: A genuine SharePoint or Dropbox share notification, sent from the real platform, pointing at a document that happens to be malicious. Because the notification really did come from the platform, it passes every check a filter can reasonably make.
settings.s20: A QR code in an attachment, because it moves the attack onto a phone where there is no filtering and no visible address bar. The message itself carries no link for anything to inspect.
settings.s22: A reply inserted into an email thread that has been running for weeks, from a supplier whose mailbox was compromised last month, so it has real history above it. Nothing about the conversation looks new or unusual.
settings.s24: The one that catches the most people. An attacker with a stolen password sits between you and Microsoft using a proxy page that looks exactly right. You type the code, and they capture the session token rather than the password. Multi-factor authentication still matters enormously, but on its own it is not the finish line people assume.
settings.s26: Filtering deals with volume. What it will not do is make a convincing message from a real supplier account look wrong, which is why authentication, monitoring and a team that knows to check unusual requests all sit alongside it.

settings.s1: The expensive one involves no malware at all
settings.s2: The most costly email attacks we deal with do not carry a payload. Someone gets into a mailbox with a working password, sits quietly and reads. They learn how your invoices are worded, who signs things off, when your finance person is on holiday. Then they send one message asking for bank details to be updated, from a real internal account, in the house style.
settings.s4: Managed detection and response
settings.s7: There is nothing for antivirus to find, because nothing was installed. The usual tell is a mailbox rule the attacker added to hide their tracks, quietly moving replies into an obscure folder so the real owner never sees the conversation happening in their name. That is why alerting on new forwarding and filing rules matters more than it sounds.
settings.s9: The control that actually stops it
settings.s10: The other half of the answer is not technical. Any request to change bank details gets verified on a phone number you already had, never one supplied in the email itself. It is a dull control that defeats a very profitable attack.

settings.s1: SPF, DKIM and DMARC, without the jargon
settings.s2: Three records that decide whether anyone can send email pretending to be you.
settings.s4: SPF
settings.s5: Lists the servers allowed to send mail for your domain. If a message arrives from somewhere not on the list, the receiver has grounds to be suspicious. It breaks quietly when you add a new sending tool, such as a mailing platform or a booking system, and nobody updates the record.
settings.s8: Signs your outgoing mail cryptographically so the receiver can confirm it genuinely came from you and was not altered on the way. It answers the question SPF cannot, which is whether the message itself is authentic rather than just the route it took.
settings.s11: Ties the two together and tells receivers what to do when a message fails. This is where most businesses stop too early. A DMARC record set to none is monitoring only, and does nothing to stop spoofing. Moving carefully to quarantine and then reject is what actually protects your domain, and it is exactly what we manage for you.

settings.s5: What does email security protect against?
settings.s6: Phishing, spam, malware, spoofing, impersonation and business email compromise across Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace. In practice the hardest of those to stop is a genuine message from a supplier whose account has been compromised, which is why filtering alone is never the whole answer.
settings.s8: It includes real capability, and a lot of what we do is configure that properly rather than sell you something on top. Defaults are permissive, impersonation protection needs your actual names and domains added, and SPF, DKIM and DMARC are your job rather than Microsoft’s. Where the built-in tooling genuinely falls short we add a layer, and we will tell you which is which.
settings.s9: What are SPF, DKIM and DMARC?
settings.s10: Three DNS records that stop attackers sending email as your domain. SPF lists who may send, DKIM signs your mail so it can be verified, and DMARC tells receivers what to do with anything that fails. Most businesses have DMARC set to monitoring only, which looks reassuring in an audit and prevents nothing. We manage the move to enforcement.
settings.s11: We have multi-factor authentication. Is that enough?
settings.s12: It is one of the most valuable things you can switch on, and it is still not sufficient by itself. Attackers now use proxy pages that capture the session after you approve the prompt, so the login succeeds without them ever knowing your password. Phishing-resistant methods, conditional access and monitoring for odd sign-ins are what close that gap.
settings.s13: Someone has already been compromised. Can you help?
settings.s14: Yes, and the order matters. Sessions get revoked and the password reset, because changing the password alone leaves an active session running. Then we look for mailbox rules the attacker added, check what was accessed and whether anything was sent in their name, and work out how they got in so it does not simply happen again.
settings.s15: Do you train our staff as well?
settings.s16: Yes. Filtering plus authentication handles most of the volume, but the attacks that get through are specifically designed to persuade a person. Security awareness training and phishing simulation are a separate service and they pair naturally with this one.

settings.s11: How attackers move through a network
settings.s13: Attacks that carry no malware at all
settings.s14: Someone gets hold of a working username and password, often from a convincing phishing page, and simply logs in. Nothing has to be installed, so nothing gets flagged. From there the attacker uses tools that are already on the machine, which is why this approach is known as living off the land. To antivirus it all looks like normal admin work.
settings.s17: MDR looks at behaviour instead of file signatures. It is less interested in what a file is called and more interested in what is happening: an account signing in from two countries an hour apart, a process quietly turning off protection, files being encrypted in bulk, a workstation suddenly scanning the rest of the network. Those patterns are hard to disguise, because they are the attack itself rather than the tooling used to deliver it.

settings.s1: Who is actually watching, and when
settings.s2: This is the question worth asking any provider, so here is our answer in plain terms. During working hours, when the security tooling raises an alert it creates a ticket in our helpdesk. It lands in the same queue our engineers already work to, and one of them picks it up and investigates. Outside those hours, monitoring and first response are handled by a specialist partner we work with, who can act on anything urgent rather than leaving it until morning.
settings.s3: A lot of providers our size imply they run their own round the clock security operations centre. Very few actually do. A small team cannot staff three shifts properly, and pretending otherwise means alerts sit unread overnight, which is exactly when ransomware tends to run. Being straight about the split matters more than sounding impressive, and it is easy for you to verify.
settings.s4: The affected device or account is contained so the problem stops spreading, then the alert is investigated properly to work out what happened and how far it got, and you get told what we found and what we did about it. What you do not get is a monthly PDF of graphs with nobody having looked at any of it.

settings.s6: Managed Detection and Response pairs security tooling with people who look at what it finds. The tooling watches for suspicious behaviour across your devices, Microsoft 365 and servers. When something looks real, a person investigates it and acts to contain it. The managed part is the bit that matters, because software on its own only produces alerts.
settings.s8: In working hours, alerts raise a ticket in our helpdesk and our own engineers investigate. Outside working hours, monitoring and first response are covered by a specialist partner who can act on anything urgent. We would rather tell you that plainly than imply we staff our own overnight security operations centre, because most providers our size do not.
settings.s9: How is MDR different from antivirus?
settings.s10: Antivirus checks whether a file matches something already known to be bad. MDR watches behaviour, which catches attacks that use no malware at all, such as someone logging in with a stolen password and using tools already present on the machine. You want both. Antivirus stops the obvious, MDR catches what walks straight past it.
settings.s11: We have Microsoft 365 Business Premium. Isn’t that enough?
settings.s12: Business Premium includes genuinely capable security tooling, and we often build on exactly that rather than selling you something extra. The gap is not the licence, it is that the alerts it generates go to nobody in particular. MDR is the layer that turns those alerts into someone investigating and responding.
settings.s13: What happens when something is detected?
settings.s14: The affected account or device is contained first so the problem stops spreading. Then it gets investigated to establish what happened, how it got in and what it reached. You are told what we found and what we did, in language you can pass to your insurer or your board without a translator.
settings.s15: Does MDR help with Cyber Essentials or cyber insurance?
settings.s16: Cyber Essentials does not require MDR, though the malware protection and secure configuration controls sit comfortably alongside it. Insurers are a different matter. Many now ask directly whether you have monitoring and response in place, and the answer can affect both your premium and whether a claim is paid. We hold Cyber Essentials certification ourselves and can take you through it.

settings.s1: What a SIEM is actually for
settings.s2: A SIEM does something quite specific: it gathers logs from everywhere, puts them into a common format, and looks for patterns across them that no single system could ever see on its own.
settings.s4: Firewall and network device logs
settings.s8: Email security and filtering events
settings.s12: Your firewall records a connection from an unfamiliar country. Microsoft 365 records a successful sign-in for a finance account. An endpoint records a script running out of a temporary folder. Individually each one is unremarkable and would never justify waking anybody. In sequence, within nine minutes, they describe an attack in progress.
settings.s14: Having logs is not using them
settings.s15: Correlation is the difference between having logs and being able to use them. Most businesses already produce all the evidence they need and simply have it scattered across six consoles that nobody compares, each retained for a different length of time, several of which quietly overwrite themselves.

settings.s1: How this differs from MDR, and who is watching
settings.s2: These two get sold interchangeably and they are not the same thing. Managed detection and response is focused: it watches endpoints and identities for behaviour that looks like an attack and acts to contain it. SIEM and SOC is wide: it collects from everything, correlates across sources, keeps the history, and gives you the evidence trail. Most businesses start with MDR because it stops incidents. SIEM earns its place when you need to see across the whole estate, or you have compliance and audit obligations to satisfy.

settings.s6: SIEM is the platform that collects logs from across your systems, normalises them and correlates events to spot patterns no single tool would catch. settings.s7: How is this different from MDR?
settings.s8: MDR is deep and narrow: endpoints and identities, watched for attack behaviour, contained when something is real. settings.s16: Retention is agreed with you, and it is worth thinking about properly rather than accepting a default. settings.s5: Isn’t a firewall enough to secure our network?
settings.s6: A firewall is essential, but it’s only the perimeter. Real security also depends on how internal access is controlled, how remote workers connect, whether devices and firmware are up to date, and how much visibility you have into traffic. We look across all of these, not just the firewall.
settings.s7: What is network segmentation and why does it matter?
settings.s8: Segmentation separates your network into zones so systems can only reach what they genuinely need. It matters because it limits how far an intruder, or a piece of malware, can move if one device is compromised, containing a problem rather than letting it spread across the business.
settings.s9: Can you secure remote and hybrid working?
settings.s10: Yes. We provide encrypted remote access with stronger authentication so your team can work securely from anywhere, without the connection becoming a weak point. It’s designed to protect the business while staying easy for staff to use.
settings.s11: How often should firewall rules be reviewed?
settings.s12: At least annually, and after any significant change such as a new site, cloud service or major project. Rules tend to accumulate over time, so regular reviews stop old, unnecessary access quietly widening your exposure.
settings.s13: Will a review disrupt our network?
settings.s14: No. Assessment work is carried out carefully and any changes are planned and agreed with you in advance, scheduled around your operations so your team and customers aren’t affected.

settings.s5: Do we still need strong passwords if we use MFA?
settings.s6: Yes. Multi-factor authentication is an excellent additional layer, but it works best alongside strong, unique passwords. Together they make accounts far harder to compromise, which is why we combine secure password management with MFA rather than relying on either alone.
settings.s7: What is a password manager and is it safe?
settings.s8: A password manager securely stores and generates complex, unique passwords so employees don’t have to remember or reuse them. Reputable business password managers encrypt credentials so only the user can access them, which is far safer than spreadsheets, documents or memorised passwords reused across systems.
settings.s9: How do you handle shared accounts?
settings.s10: Shared accounts are common but risky because they reduce accountability. We introduce stronger controls and secure sharing so teams can access what they need without exposing the actual passwords, and so you can see who has access to what.
settings.s11: Will this slow down our team’s access?
settings.s12: No, done well, it speeds things up. A password manager fills credentials automatically, so staff spend less time resetting forgotten passwords. Our aim is security that improves usability rather than getting in the way of everyday work.
settings.s13: Is this a one-off project or ongoing?
settings.s14: We can introduce secure password management as a project, then provide ongoing reviews, password policy, user access management and multi-factor authentication reviews, so account security keeps pace as your business, team and cloud applications change.

settings.s1: Operational resilience is a regulatory expectation, not an IT preference
settings.s2: Financial services firms are held to a standard of resilience that most businesses are not. Since March 2022 FCA-regulated firms have been expected to identify their important business services, set impact tolerances for disruption and be able to show they can stay within them. That obligation reaches directly into IT.
settings.s4: Your IT provider is inside the regulatory perimeter
settings.s5: The FCA expects firms to oversee outsourced arrangements rather than delegate the risk with the work. In practice that means your provider should be able to answer questions about access control, change management, incident response and where data physically sits, in writing and without a scramble. We keep that documentation current because it is asked for, not because it is a nice extra.
settings.s8: Communications retention, journalling and immutable copies are requirements before they are features, and they change how mailboxes, archives and backups should be configured. Getting this right at design time is far cheaper than reconstructing history later.
settings.s10: Testing the recovery, not just the backup
settings.s11: An impact tolerance you have never tested is an assumption. We would rather rehearse a restore against a defined recovery time and find the gaps in a planned exercise than discover them during an incident.
settings.s14: Regulators have grown wary of firms depending on a single provider for everything, and the same logic applies to the platforms underneath. Knowing which single points of failure exist between your desk and your client’s money, and having a documented answer for each, is a more useful exercise than adding another tool. We would rather map that honestly and tell you where the exposure sits than pretend a monitoring dashboard removes it.

settings.s2: Insurance businesses hold an unusual concentration of sensitive personal data and, in health and protection lines, special-category data too. They also occupy an awkward position: a broker whose systems are down is unavailable at exactly the moment a client needs to notify a claim.

settings.s5: Workload arrives in bursts around renewal dates and after weather events, and capacity has to be there on the day rather than on average. Monitoring that only reports monthly uptime will miss the hour that actually mattered.

settings.s8: Quoting, binding and claims handling all run through a mix of broker software and insurer extranets, each with its own authentication and browser quirks. Keeping that estate stable, patched and accessible is most of the practical support work in this sector.
settings.s10: Special-category data raises the bar on access
settings.s11: Where medical or health information is held, the standard for who can see what stops being a matter of tidiness and becomes a matter of lawful basis. Role-based access, logging and reviewed permissions are the mechanics that make that defensible.
settings.s13: Delegated authority means someone else’s data on your systems
settings.s14: MGAs and brokers operating under delegated authority hold data the insurer remains accountable for, which means the insurer’s own assurance requirements land on your infrastructure. Expect questions about encryption, retention periods, sub-processors and breach notification timelines, and expect them in a questionnaire rather than a conversation. Having those answers documented in advance turns a two-week scramble into an afternoon.

settings.s1: What makes IT different in a law firm
settings.s2: A practice runs on confidentiality, an audit trail and files that have to survive for decades. That combination puts different demands on IT than almost any other professional service, and it is where most generic support arrangements fall short.
settings.s4: Payment redirection fraud targets conveyancers directly
settings.s5: Interception of completion emails and last-minute changes of bank details is one of the most common frauds aimed at law firms, and it arrives through the mailbox rather than the firewall. The controls that matter are email authentication, impersonation protection, tight rules on who can change payment information, and training that teaches fee earners to verify by phone against a known number.
settings.s7: Retention measured in decades, not years
settings.s8: Wills, deeds and matter files often have to be produced long after the matter closed and long after the software that created them was retired. That is an archiving question rather than a backup question: readable formats, documented restore paths, and storage you can still search in fifteen years.
settings.s10: Case and practice management sits at the centre
settings.s11: Time recording, matter files and the client account all live in the practice management system, so its availability effectively sets the firm’s working hours. We manage the platforms and infrastructure around it, keep the integrations and access working, and treat downtime there as a first-priority incident.

settings.s1: Two networks, one business: the office and the shop floor
settings.s2: Manufacturers run two quite different technology estates. The office side looks like any other business. The production side runs machine controllers, PLCs and inspection equipment, often on operating systems that cannot be patched and were never designed to be on a network at all.
settings.s4: Segmentation instead of upgrading the unupgradeable
settings.s5: A press brake or CNC controller running an unsupported Windows version usually cannot be updated without invalidating the machine’s support agreement. The workable answer is to isolate it: a separate network segment, tightly controlled routes in and out, and monitoring on the boundary rather than on the machine.
settings.s7: Downtime has a per-hour price and everyone knows it
settings.s8: In an office, a slow morning is an irritation. On a line, stoppage has a number attached and it is usually already calculated. That changes the priority conversation: resilience spending on the things that halt production is far easier to justify than a general upgrade.
settings.s10: Coverage across a shop floor is a physical problem
settings.s11: Steel racking, machinery and vehicle movement break wireless coverage in ways an office survey never predicts. Scanners, tablets and terminals need a network designed for the building as it actually is, which means surveying the space rather than assuming it.

settings.s1: Findings are only useful if they are ranked

settings.s4: Where the estate stops matching the paperwork
settings.s5: Almost every audit turns up the same category of surprise: devices nobody can account for, accounts belonging to people who left, software still installed after the project that needed it finished, and a licence count that no longer matches headcount. None of this is negligence. It is what happens when a business grows faster than its record-keeping. Establishing an accurate baseline is most of the value, because every later decision depends on knowing what you actually have.
settings.s7: Risk that is real versus risk that is theoretical
settings.s8: A vulnerability on an internal print server behind a firewall is not the same as an exposed remote access service with a shared password, even if a scanner scores them similarly. Context decides severity: what the system touches, who can reach it, and what happens if it stops. We rank findings by that rather than by raw score, so effort goes where it changes the outcome.
settings.s10: The processes matter as much as the technology
settings.s11: How a new starter gets their accounts, how a leaver loses them, who approves a change, and whether anyone checks the backup restored are all process questions that no scan detects. They are also where most real incidents begin. An audit that only looks at boxes and software misses the half of the picture that people actually operate.

settings.s14: Findings are written to be read by a director as well as an engineer, with the reasoning visible rather than a bare list of severities. settings.s1: How a managed Mac fleet actually works
settings.s2: Most Mac problems in a business are not really Mac problems. They are the result of nobody managing the devices centrally.
settings.s4: Zero-touch setup
settings.s5: With Apple Business Manager and automated device enrolment, a Mac bought for a new starter can be shipped straight to them. It enrols itself the first time it is switched on, applies your settings, installs the apps they need and lands ready to work. Nobody has to sit and build it, and nobody has to post it to us first.
settings.s8: Configuration profiles let us set the things that matter once and have them hold across every device: full-disk encryption on, the firewall enabled, a sensible screen lock, and administrator rights given deliberately rather than by default. New Macs inherit the same standard automatically.
settings.s11: macOS releases, browsers and business apps are kept current on a schedule instead of whenever someone gets round to clicking the prompt. When a device is lost, or someone leaves, it can be locked or wiped remotely and the licences reclaimed rather than quietly disappearing.

settings.s1: Mixed environments break on identity, not hardware
settings.s2: Hardly any business runs on one platform only. Designers and developers want Macs, finance and operations are on Windows, and the two have to share the same files, the same email and the same security rules. When that goes wrong, it is almost never because the hardware cannot cope. It is because identity and file access were never joined up.
settings.s4: Our managed cloud services
settings.s7: The fix is to stop treating Macs as visitors on the network. Connect them to the same directory everyone else uses, so a Mac user signs in with the same Microsoft 365 account, the same multi-factor authentication applies, and revoking access when someone leaves genuinely revokes it everywhere.
settings.s9: Files, printing and the awkward bits
settings.s10: Keep shared files in SharePoint and OneDrive rather than a legacy file share, which is where cross-platform setups usually start to creak. Then test the practical things on both platforms instead of assuming they work. Printing, VPN and conditional access are the usual culprits.
settings.s12: Handled by us, not a reseller chain
settings.s13: We are a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider, so the Microsoft 365 and Entra ID side is handled directly by us rather than through a reseller chain, and the Mac side is managed to the same standard as the PCs beside it.

settings.s2: The idea that Macs do not get malware is comfortably out of date. macOS is actively targeted, most commonly by information stealers dressed up as legitimate installers or browser downloads, which go after saved passwords, browser sessions and crypto wallets. The delivery method is usually a person being persuaded to run something, which is exactly why endpoint protection and user awareness both matter.

settings.s5: FileVault full-disk encryption enforced and key escrow held

settings.s13: What macOS already does for you
settings.s14: macOS does ship with some solid defences of its own. Gatekeeper and notarisation check what is allowed to run, XProtect removes known malicious software, and System Integrity Protection stops much of the operating system being tampered with. Those are a solid floor, not a managed security programme. None of them tell you that a device has stopped receiving updates, that encryption was switched off, or that someone has been granted admin rights they should not have.
settings.s16: Cyber Essentials applies to Macs too
settings.s17: The five Cyber Essentials controls apply to Macs exactly as they apply to Windows: firewalls, secure configuration, user access control, malware protection and patch management. We hold Cyber Essentials certification ourselves and take clients through it, and Macs are assessed alongside everything else rather than quietly left out of scope.

Managed endpoint protection adds the central visibility and alerting that distinguishes a protected fleet from a set of individually hopeful laptops.
settings.s14: Yes. settings.s32: Birmingham is one of the closer locations to our Stevenage base, so where hardware genuinely needs attention a same-working-day visit is a realistic commitment rather than a hopeful one. For manufacturers in the wider West Midlands, that is often the deciding factor.
settings.s35: Sustained construction and relocation activity
settings.s36: Large-scale infrastructure and development work across the city has kept commercial relocation unusually frequent. Moves are where IT most often goes wrong, and the recurring cause is connectivity lead times booked too late rather than anything technical.
settings.s39: Several sites should still mean one identity
settings.s40: Operating across the conurbation often means each location grew its own arrangements, with separate logins, separate file stores and separate ways of doing things. Consolidating to a single identity per person, with access granted by role, removes most of the friction people feel when they move between sites and removes the accounts that accumulate when someone changes location. It also makes leavers a single action rather than a checklist per building.
settings.s43: Project sites open and close, and IT has to match
settings.s44: Where work runs on a project basis, sites appear for a period and then stand down. Treating connectivity, hardware and access as something to set up and recover repeatedly, with a standard build rather than a bespoke one each time, keeps mobilisation quick and stops equipment quietly disappearing at the end of a job. The cost of a standard kit list is recovered the second time it is used.

settings.s19: Budgets that expect the spend to be defensible
settings.s20: Owner-managed firms tend to ask what a line item prevents before approving it, which is a fair question. We would rather cost the things that stop the business working and be honest that the rest can wait than present a package where nothing is optional.
settings.s23: Production and office IT sharing one network
settings.s24: In smaller manufacturers the office switch and the machine on the floor are frequently the same network, because it grew that way. Separating them is usually the single highest-value piece of work available, and it rarely requires new hardware.
settings.s27: Working across Bradford and Leeds as one business
settings.s28: Staff moving between sites in the same week need their files, phone extension and permissions to follow them. That is an identity and cloud question rather than a networking one, and it is cheaper to solve properly than to work around.
settings.s31: Onsite attendance is a planned journey, not a call-out
settings.s32: Our engineers are based in Stevenage and travel north, so a Bradford visit is arranged rather than immediate. In practice most faults are resolved remotely long before a visit would arrive, and we would rather be straight about the travel than describe ourselves as local.
settings.s35: Older building stock shapes what is physically possible
settings.s36: Much of Bradford’s commercial space is in converted mill and older industrial buildings, where thick stone walls, long cable runs and limited riser access constrain what a network can do. Wireless surveys in these buildings routinely produce different answers from the floorplan, and cabling work is often the unglamorous prerequisite to everything else.
settings.s39: Machines usually outlive the software that drives them
settings.s40: A press or a production line bought fifteen years ago is often still perfectly serviceable, and still controlled by a PC running something no longer supported. Replacing the machine to solve a software problem is not a sensible answer. Isolating that PC on its own network segment, removing its need for internet access, and backing up its configuration is the pragmatic one. The goal is that an unsupported system cannot be reached from the office network and cannot reach anything else.
settings.s43: Backups that only cover the office miss the production data
settings.s44: Office files are usually protected because they live in a cloud platform somebody manages. Production data frequently is not: machine configurations, job files, quality records and the small local database on the shop floor PC that nobody thinks of as a server. Those are the things that make a rebuild slow when hardware fails. Listing what a full recovery would actually require, then checking each item is covered, is a job worth doing once and reviewing yearly.

settings.s3: Bradford’s business base leans towards manufacturing and owner-managed firms, sitting close enough to Leeds that many firms operate across both. It is a market where IT spend has to visibly earn itself rather than being taken on trust.
settings.s4: That is a fair test and managed IT stands up to it: fewer outages because problems are caught by monitoring first, a service desk that resolves most issues remotely on the same working day, and one predictable monthly cost instead of unpredictable emergency invoices.

settings.s27: City-centre growth means frequent moves and fit-outs

settings.s35: A health and public-sector technology cluster
settings.s36: Leeds has an established concentration of health-related and public-sector digital organisations alongside its financial and legal core. Suppliers into that ecosystem are routinely asked to evidence security controls and data handling formally, which makes documentation part of the deliverable rather than an afterthought.
settings.s39: Retention is a records decision before it is a storage one
settings.s40: Regulated firms carry obligations about how long client records are kept and how they are produced if asked. That is a policy question, but it lands as a technology one: retention rules on mailboxes and document libraries, a legal hold that survives an employee leaving, and a search that can actually find everything on a matter. Setting it deliberately is straightforward. Reconstructing it later, from mailboxes people have tidied and archives nobody documented, is the expensive version.
settings.s43: Sending client documents by attachment is the habit worth breaking
settings.s44: The safest change most professional firms can make is to stop moving sensitive documents as email attachments. A portal or a secure share means access can be withdrawn, viewing is recorded, and a message sent to the wrong recipient does not hand over the file. It also removes the temptation to protect a document with a password sent in a second email, which is not protection at all if both messages reach the same inbox.

settings.s35: A workforce that is often multilingual and shift-based
settings.s36: Manufacturing and distribution employers in the city frequently run diverse, multilingual teams on shared terminals across shifts. That pushes the design towards individual accounts on shared devices, clear session handling and security training that works for people who do not sit at a desk all day.
settings.s39: The stock system, not email, is the one that must not stop
settings.s40: Where distribution and light manufacturing are involved, priorities usually need reordering. Email being slow is an irritation; the warehouse system being unavailable stops picking, dispatch and invoicing at once. That should be reflected in what is monitored most closely, what is covered by the highest response priority, and what has a tested fallback. It is worth writing down which systems genuinely halt trading, because the answer is rarely the one people assume.
settings.s43: Taking card payments pulls part of the network into scope
settings.s44: Retail and wholesale operations that take card payments inherit obligations about how those systems are separated from everything else. The practical work is keeping payment devices off the same flat network as the office machines and the warehouse kit, so the questions a bank or an assessor asks have a clear answer. Doing that when the network is next touched costs very little; retrofitting segmentation across a live site is a different job entirely.

settings.s2: Greater Manchester combines a professional-services core, a well-established media and broadcast cluster, and one of the larger digital and tech scenes in the UK. Each brings a different bottleneck, and they rarely overlap.

settings.s19: Media work is a storage and bandwidth problem first
settings.s20: Production files are large, versioned and edited collaboratively, which strains both the connection and the backup window. Getting the storage tiering and sync rules right matters more here than raw device specification.
settings.s23: Fast-growing teams outgrow their IT decisions quickly
settings.s24: A structure that suited twelve people becomes the constraint at forty, usually showing up as shared logins and permissions nobody can explain. Building identity and access properly early is far cheaper than untangling it later.
settings.s27: A city region, not a single city
settings.s28: Businesses commonly operate across Manchester, Salford, Stockport and Trafford. The aim is one consistent standard across all of them rather than separate arrangements that diverge over time.
settings.s31: Onsite work planned, remote work the norm
settings.s32: Our engineers travel from London and Stevenage, so Manchester visits are arranged rather than same-day. For the professional, digital and media businesses that make up much of the city’s base, this is rarely the constraint people expect, because the work is cloud-hosted and the faults are resolvable remotely.
settings.s35: Co-working and serviced space is unusually common
settings.s36: A large share of Manchester’s smaller businesses sit in shared or serviced buildings where the network belongs to the landlord. That removes several options entirely and makes device-level security, identity controls and cellular failover more important than anything that assumes control of the router.
settings.s39: Short-term collaborators need scoped access, not a full account
settings.s40: Agency, production and digital work runs on people who are involved for one project. Giving each of them a full account with broad access is quick and creates a long tail of dormant logins. Guest access scoped to a single workspace or folder, with an expiry, covers almost every case and leaves nothing behind when the work finishes. It is also far easier to answer a client question about who could see their material.
settings.s43: Archive and backup solve different problems
settings.s44: Finished work that must be retrievable in three years is an archive question. Recovering yesterday’s state after something went wrong is a backup question. Using one for the other is where costs and disappointment come from, either paying premium storage to hold completed projects indefinitely, or discovering the backup retention window closed long before anyone came looking. Deciding which material is which, once, makes both cheaper and more reliable.

In practice this makes remote resolution and good remote tooling more important, and it makes us more careful about specifying hardware that will not need hands on it.
settings.s23: Engineering and design workloads are heavier than office ones
settings.s24: CAD and simulation work needs specification and storage that ordinary office procurement underestimates, and the files are large enough to change how backup is designed.
settings.s27: Resilience matters more when help is further away
settings.s28: Where a visit takes longer, spare capacity and a documented recovery path are worth more than they would be in a city with an engineer twenty minutes away. That is a design decision, not an upsell.
settings.s31: Marine, offshore and energy engineering data
settings.s32: Work connected to the Tyne brings survey, inspection and design datasets that are large, retained for long periods and often gathered somewhere with poor connectivity before being brought back. That makes staged transfer and disciplined archiving more relevant than day-to-day office bandwidth.
settings.s35: Contact-centre style operations depend on the call path
settings.s36: Where a business runs telephone-based teams, availability of the voice path and its underlying connection is the service. Monitoring that reports on the network but not on call quality will miss the fault the business actually experiences.
settings.s39: Working offshore or on site means designing for intermittent links
settings.s40: Staff on a vessel, a rig or a remote site are not continuously connected, and treating that as a fault to be fixed usually fails. The better assumption is that work happens offline and synchronises when a link is available, with conflict handling that does not silently discard someone’s changes. It also affects security choices, since a control that depends on reaching a server in real time will lock out the person who most needs access.
settings.s43: Large engineering files need version discipline, not just space
settings.s44: Design and modelling work produces large files that several people revise. The failure mode is rarely running out of storage; it is two people working from different copies, or a reference file moving so an assembly no longer resolves. Check-out behaviour, a clear structure for references, and backups that capture a coherent point in time across the whole set are what prevent a day of rework.

settings.s1: What we account for across Wales
settings.s2: Wales is a coverage question as much as a technical one. The distance between Cardiff, Swansea, mid Wales and the north is considerable, connectivity is uneven outside the urban areas, and there is a language requirement that does not apply elsewhere in our coverage.

settings.s19: Connectivity cannot be assumed outside the cities
settings.s20: Fixed-line options in rural and valley locations are frequently limited, and mobile coverage varies within a few miles. Designing for the connection that exists, with cellular failover and offline-tolerant working where needed, beats specifying for the connection you wish were there.
settings.s23: Welsh language obligations reach into everyday systems
settings.s24: Organisations providing public-facing services may need to offer Welsh alongside English, which affects templates, forms, signatures and locale settings across the estate. Building it in from the start avoids a retrofit.
settings.s27: Supplying the public sector brings its requirements with it
settings.s28: A large share of Welsh business touches the public sector somewhere, whether that is a health board, a local authority or a Welsh Government programme. Those relationships tend to pass their assurance expectations down the chain, so the questions arrive in a procurement pack rather than from your own risk register: how access is controlled, where data is held, what your recovery position is, and whether you hold a recognised certification. Being able to answer without a scramble is usually the difference between staying on a framework and quietly dropping off it.
settings.s31: Onsite attendance across Wales is planned work
settings.s32: Because our engineers travel from London and Stevenage, a visit to west or north Wales is scheduled rather than same-day. We would rather set that expectation at the outset than imply a call-out radius we cannot honour. It also changes how we specify: more emphasis on remote diagnostics, on hardware that is unlikely to need physical attention, and on spare capacity held locally where a failure would stop the business.
settings.s35: Seasonal and dispersed operating patterns
settings.s36: Tourism, hospitality and agriculture give parts of Wales a pronounced seasonal shape, with headcount and transaction volumes that swing through the year. Licensing and capacity that suit August are wasteful in February, and the reverse causes outages. Reviewing that annually rather than renewing on autopilot usually saves more than any single technical change.
settings.s39: Sites with unreliable connectivity need to keep working offline
settings.s40: Where a connection is intermittent rather than slow, the design question changes from bandwidth to tolerance. Systems that assume constant connectivity will fail badly on a poor line, whereas ones that hold work locally and reconcile later will not. Choosing software that behaves sensibly offline, and keeping a mobile fallback that engages automatically, tends to matter more at a rural site than any upgrade to the primary line.
settings.s43: Seasonal hiring is an identity problem in disguise
settings.s44: Businesses that scale up for a season need dozens of people productive quickly and gone cleanly afterwards. Done informally that means shared logins and accounts nobody closes. A prepared template for a seasonal role, created on arrival and expiring at the end of the contract, takes the same effort the first time and almost none thereafter, while leaving a clear record of who had access and when.

settings.s2: Managed IT for businesses across Wales
settings.s3: Wales spreads a lot of business activity across a wide geography, from the M4 corridor to sites where the nearest town is a drive away. Connectivity and remote working therefore matter more here than in a dense city centre, and manufacturing and public-sector-adjacent work make up a healthy share of the mix.
settings.s4: Support built around remote-first working suits that well. Our service desk resolves most issues remotely, usually the same working day, and where a site genuinely needs an engineer, one travels to you with a same-working-day aim.

settings.s11: RTO: time you can be down
settings.s12: Why both come first
settings.s14: How much work can you afford to lose? That is your recovery point objective. If backups run nightly, your RPO is up to 24 hours, which means a failure at four in the afternoon costs you the whole day. For a finance team mid month that might be genuinely serious. For other work it is an annoyance. Only you can say which.
settings.s16: How long can you be down? That is your recovery time objective. Restoring a large fileserver from cloud storage is not quick, and if the honest answer is two days while the business needs four hours, no amount of backup software fixes that. The design has to change instead, usually towards replication or standby systems for the handful of things that genuinely cannot wait.
settings.s18: Get those two numbers agreed and everything else follows from them. Skip them and you end up with backups that technically exist and a recovery that takes a week, which is the situation most businesses are quietly in.

settings.s1: Your backup is a target, not a safety net
settings.s2: Ransomware crews worked out years ago that encrypting live data is only half a job. If the victim can restore, they do not pay. So the backups get attacked first, and the tools people rely on most are the ones sitting on the same network with the same administrator credentials.
settings.s4: How ransomware targets backups
settings.s7: At least one copy has to be somewhere the attacker cannot touch. Immutable storage that cannot be altered or deleted for a set period, separate credentials that are not the ones your domain admin uses daily, and multi-factor authentication on the backup console itself. The old three copies, two media, one offsite rule still holds up, with the modern addition that one copy should be genuinely unchangeable.
settings.s10: Attackers commonly sit inside a network for weeks before triggering anything. If your retention is short, your clean restore point may already have been deleted by the time you need it. Retention is a security decision, not just a storage cost.

settings.s1: Microsoft 365 is not backing up your data
settings.s2: This one catches out well-run businesses regularly. Microsoft keeps your service running and protects its own infrastructure. It does not keep a point-in-time copy of your data for you to roll back to, and its own shared responsibility model says so plainly.
settings.s4: Microsoft 365 backup
settings.s6: Why retention policies are not backups
settings.s7: Retention policies, litigation hold and the recycle bin help within limited windows, and none of them give you what you actually want at the worst moment, which is the ability to say put this mailbox, or this SharePoint site, back exactly as it was on Tuesday morning. Deleted items age out. A user with permissions can destroy a lot of shared content quickly, and ransomware syncing through OneDrive will happily do the same.
settings.s10: The fix is unglamorous and cheap relative to the risk: an independent backup of Microsoft 365 or Google Workspace, held separately from the platform itself, with retention you have actually chosen rather than inherited.

settings.s0: What drifts if nobody owns it
settings.s1: A tenant does not stay tidy on its own
settings.s2: Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace are set up once, usually carefully, and then reality happens. People join and leave, someone shares a folder to get a job done on a Friday, a trial licence quietly becomes a renewal, an app gets granted access and is never looked at again. None of it is negligence. It is what a live system does when no one has been given the job of tending it.
settings.s4: Leavers who never fully left
settings.s5: Offboarding usually gets the obvious part right, which is disabling the sign-in. What tends to survive is everything attached to that person: files owned by their account, a shared mailbox they still have rights to, an app password issued years ago, a personal device still enrolled. The tidy version archives the mailbox, transfers ownership of their files to a named colleague, revokes tokens and sessions rather than only the password, and then releases the licence. Done in that order, nothing is lost and nothing is left open.
settings.s7: Licences bought for a headcount you no longer have
settings.s8: The common pattern is paying for more seats than people, while some of the people you do have sit on a licence tier above what their role needs, and a handful sit below what they actually use. Reviewing assignment against real usage two or three times a year usually pays for the review several times over. As a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider we can adjust your licensing directly rather than sending you to a portal to work it out yourself.
settings.s10: Sharing links that outlived their purpose
settings.s11: Anyone-with-the-link sharing is genuinely useful and genuinely hard to retire, because the link keeps working long after the project ends and nobody remembers creating it. Expiry dates on external shares, a periodic report of what is shared outside the business, and a default that favours named access over open links keep this manageable without making collaboration painful.
settings.s14: Someone signs in to a tool with their work account and grants it permission to read mail or files. That consent persists whether or not the tool is still in use, and it is not visible unless somebody looks. Reviewing granted permissions and deciding whether users can consent on their own behalf is a small piece of configuration that closes a route people rarely think about.

settings.s1: The bin empties, and that is by design
settings.s2: Google Workspace is genuinely resilient. Your data is replicated, the service stays up, and hardware failure is not something you need to think about. That is availability, and Google is clear that it is what they are responsible for. Retention is a different question, and the answer is a countdown rather than an archive.
settings.s4: Deletion is on a timer, not a shelf
settings.s5: Items removed from Gmail or Drive sit in trash for a limited period and are then purged. An administrator has a further short window to recover some of it, and after that the copy is gone rather than archived somewhere deeper. Most data loss we are called about is not dramatic: someone tidied a shared folder in good faith, and the discovery came weeks later when a colleague went looking for a file.
settings.s7: A departing employee takes their Drive with them
settings.s8: Files in a personal My Drive belong to that account. Suspend or delete the account without transferring ownership first and the files go with it, including anything they had shared with the team, which stops resolving for everyone else. Shared Drives avoid this because the team owns the content rather than an individual, but almost every business has years of work sitting in personal Drives regardless.
settings.s10: A compromised account deletes on purpose
settings.s11: Accidental deletion is recoverable within the window. Deliberate deletion by someone who has taken over an account is designed to defeat exactly that, and emptying the trash is part of it. This is the case that separates a backup from a retention policy: an independent copy sits outside the account, so nothing done inside it can reach the copy.
settings.s14: Drive for desktop keeps local and cloud copies in step, which is the point of it. If files are encrypted on the laptop, the sync does its job and carries the damage upward. Point-in-time restore is what gets you back to the state before the change, rather than trying to unpick which version of which file is intact.

settings.s2: The test is the restore, not the backup
settings.s3: Backups fail quietly. They run, they report success, and the problem only shows up on the day someone needs a file back. That is why the measure worth caring about is whether a restore has actually been performed recently, not whether the job is green.
settings.s4: What we look for is granular recovery, so a single message or one folder can come back without restoring an entire account; coverage across Gmail, Drive, Shared Drives, Contacts and Calendar rather than mail alone; a retention period long enough that a deletion noticed months later is still recoverable; and a copy held independently of the Workspace tenant, so a compromise of the tenant cannot reach it.

settings.s2: Azure is pay as you go, which sounds reassuring until the first bill arrives that nobody can explain. It is almost never one big mistake. It is a dozen small ones nobody owned.

settings.s12: Virtual machines get sized generously during a project and never revisited, so you pay for headroom you have never touched. Test environments spin up on a Tuesday and run all weekend because switching them off was somebody’s job in principle.
settings.s15: Disks and public IP addresses outlive the machines they belonged to and keep billing quietly on their own. Nothing is tagged, so when the bill goes up nobody can say which project or department caused it.
settings.s18: Running everything at pay as you go rates when the workload is clearly permanent is the most common overspend we find. Reservations and savings plans exist precisely for predictable workloads, and applying them properly is often the single biggest reduction available without changing a thing technically.
settings.s20: It just needs looking at
settings.s21: None of this needs heroics. It needs somebody looking every month, which is what management means in practice rather than in a brochure.

settings.s1: The five things we actually do in Azure
settings.s2: This is the work we get asked for, so it is the work the page is about.
settings.s4: Migration
settings.s5: Moving servers and workloads off ageing on-premise hardware. Some things lift and shift unchanged, others are better re-platformed on the way across, and a few are genuinely better left where they are. We will tell you which is which rather than moving everything because it is billable.
settings.s8: Monitoring, patching, backups verified, capacity reviewed and spend examined every month. Right-sizing, reservations and switching off what nobody is using. This is the part that decides whether Azure saves you money or quietly costs more than the servers did.
settings.s11: Identity first, because in Azure identity is the perimeter. Conditional access, multi-factor authentication, privileged access controlled rather than permanent, network segmentation, and alerting that reaches a human. We are Cyber Essentials Certified and apply the same standards here.
settings.s14: Backups configured, retained to a period you have actually chosen, held so ransomware cannot reach them, and tested by restoring rather than by looking at a green tick. Recovery objectives agreed per workload up front.
settings.s17: Azure Virtual Desktop where it genuinely fits, which is more often than people expect and less often than the marketing suggests. See below for the honest version.
settings.s20: As a Microsoft Cloud Solution Provider your licensing, support and escalation come direct from us rather than through a reseller chain, so when something needs Microsoft it goes to Microsoft.

settings.s2: Azure Virtual Desktop earns its place in specific situations, and it is worth being clear about which. It is excellent when you need people working on company systems from equipment you do not control, so contractors, offshore teams, personal machines and anyone using their own laptop. It keeps the data in Azure rather than on the endpoint, which is a genuine security win. It suits a legacy application that refuses to behave on modern desktops. It is also the fastest way to onboard twenty people at once without waiting on hardware.
settings.s4: Cloud migration services
settings.s9: It is excellent when you need people working on company systems from equipment you do not control, so contractors, offshore teams, personal machines and anyone using their own laptop. It keeps the data in Azure rather than on the endpoint. It also suits a legacy application that refuses to behave on modern desktops, and it is the fastest way to onboard twenty people without waiting on hardware.
settings.s11: It is not automatically cheaper than buying laptops. Session hosts are virtual machines and they bill while they run, so the cost case depends entirely on sizing them properly and letting autoscale shut capacity down outside working hours. Get that wrong and you have bought an expensive way to run Windows. Profiles matter too, because user data has to live somewhere sensible or logins slow to a crawl, which is what FSLogix profile containers are for.
settings.s13: If you already have Microsoft 365 Business Premium or a Windows E3 or E5 plan, the desktop entitlement is typically already included, so you are paying Azure for the compute and storage rather than buying a whole new product. We will work out whether the numbers land in your favour before recommending it, and say so if they do not.

settings.s7: Can you actually control Azure costs?
settings.s8: Yes, and it is usually the quickest win available. Right-sizing machines that were sized for a worst case, shutting down test environments out of hours, removing orphaned disks and IP addresses, and applying reservations or savings plans to workloads that clearly run permanently. Then tagging everything so the next bill can be explained without a forensic exercise.
settings.s9: Is Azure cheaper than our own servers?
settings.s10: Not automatically, and anyone who promises that without looking at your workloads is guessing. Azure wins clearly on variable demand, disaster recovery, avoiding a large hardware purchase, and anything you need to scale quickly. A steady predictable workload can cost more in Azure if it is left on pay as you go rates and never reviewed. The honest answer comes from modelling your actual usage.
settings.s11: Can you migrate our servers to Azure?
settings.s12: Yes, from a single workload up to your whole estate. Some servers move unchanged, some are better rebuilt on the way over, and occasionally the right answer is that something stays where it is for now. We work that out during discovery rather than moving everything and sorting it out later.
settings.s13: Is Azure Virtual Desktop right for us?
settings.s14: It depends on the problem you are solving. It is strong for unmanaged or personal devices, contractors, keeping data off endpoints, awkward legacy applications and onboarding quickly. It is weaker as a straight cost saving against buying laptops, because session hosts bill while they run. If you already have Business Premium or Windows E3 or E5 the desktop entitlement is usually included, which changes the maths considerably.
settings.s15: How do you secure an Azure environment?
settings.s16: Starting with identity, because that is the real perimeter. Multi-factor authentication enforced, conditional access, administrative rights granted temporarily rather than held permanently, and network segmentation so one compromised machine cannot reach everything. Then monitoring that produces a ticket a person picks up, and backups an attacker cannot reach.

settings.s5: Plasterboard is nearly transparent to Wi-Fi; concrete, foil-backed insulation, plant rooms, lift shafts and metal racking are not. settings.s1: Having a firewall is not the same as being protected
settings.s2: Almost every business we assess already owns a capable firewall. The box is rarely the issue. What it is running, and who last looked at it, usually is.
settings.s3: Firewall vulnerabilities get published, and because these devices sit on the public internet they are scanned and exploited quickly, sometimes within days of an advisory. An unpatched firewall is not a neutral risk, it is an internet-facing door with a known key. Yet firmware updates get deferred because nobody wants to reboot the internet during working hours, and then the deferral becomes permanent.
settings.s4: Somebody opened a port temporarily for a supplier in 2021 and it is still open. An any to any rule went in to get a project finished and never came out. Nobody can say which rules are still needed because there is no record of why they were added, so nobody dares remove any of them.

settings.s4: Application awareness
settings.s5: Older firewalls made decisions on ports. Modern traffic mostly rides over 443, so port rules tell you almost nothing. Application control identifies what is really passing through, which is how you allow a service you sanction while blocking one you do not, even though both look identical from the outside.
settings.s8: Inspects traffic for known exploit patterns and blocks them in transit. It is one of the licensed features that quietly stops working when a subscription lapses, which is why we track renewals as part of the service rather than leaving it to a diary entry.
settings.s11: Most threats now arrive over encrypted connections, so a firewall that cannot look inside them is guessing. It is worth being straight about the trade-offs: inspection costs throughput, needs certificates deploying properly, and some traffic such as banking should be excluded deliberately. Done carelessly it breaks applications, which is why it is configured deliberately rather than switched on wholesale.

settings.s1: VPN, or something better than VPN
settings.s2: Traditional VPN does one thing: it puts a remote device on your network. That was fine when the alternative was nothing, and it is now the part of the setup attackers most want to reach, because one stolen laptop or one reused password buys them the whole internal network to explore.

A user is authenticated, their device is checked, and they are connected to the one system they need and nothing else. If that account is later compromised, the damage is bounded by design instead of by luck. Not every business needs to move immediately, but if your VPN currently drops everyone onto a flat internal network, that is worth revisiting.

settings.s1: Two lines are not resilience if they share a duct
settings.s2: Buying a second connection feels like buying resilience, and often is not. If both circuits run from the same exchange, along the same route, or terminate on the same piece of your equipment, one contractor with a digger takes out both. Diversity has to be designed rather than assumed.
settings.s4: Diverse carrier, diverse route, diverse hardware
settings.s5: Genuine resilience means the two services do not share a failure point: different providers where possible, physically different routes into the building, and separate terminating equipment. Where a truly diverse fixed route is not available at a site, 4G or 5G backup gives you a path that fails independently by definition, because it does not use the ground at all.
settings.s7: Failover that happens before anyone notices
settings.s8: The value is in how fast and how quietly the switch happens. A failover that drops every call and every session is better than an outage, but only just. SD-WAN monitors the health of each path continuously and moves traffic when a link degrades, not only when it dies completely, which matters because slow and lossy is more common than fully down.
settings.s10: Not all traffic deserves the same treatment
settings.s11: A voice call is ruined by 100ms of jitter that a file upload would never notice. Policy-based routing lets you put real-time traffic on the most stable path and bulk transfers on the cheaper one, and change that automatically when conditions shift. This is the part that a straight second line cannot do at all.
settings.s13: Bandwidth is rarely the actual problem
settings.s14: Most sites that feel slow are not short of bandwidth. They are suffering from contention at peak times, a saturated upload path, or one backup job running in business hours. Measuring before upgrading usually costs less than upgrading, and sometimes shows the circuit was never the constraint.

settings.s12: Cat6, Cat6a and fibre optic cabling

settings.s2: Cabling faults rarely announce themselves. They surface as a call that drops once a day, a machine that negotiates at a tenth of its speed, or a camera that goes offline when the heating runs. Because the symptoms look like software, teams often spend weeks in the wrong place before anyone tests the cable.
settings.s4: Certification is not the same as it works today
settings.s5: A tester that lights up green confirms continuity. Certification measures the things that actually degrade performance: crosstalk, return loss, attenuation and length, against the standard for the category installed. It is also the only evidence that the installation met specification on the day, which matters when a fault appears two years later and nobody can agree what was installed.
settings.s7: Category choice is a decision about the next decade
settings.s8: Cabling outlives several generations of the equipment plugged into it, so the sensible question is not what today’s switches need but what the building will need before it is next refitted. The cost difference between categories is small next to the cost of pulling cable through an occupied building a second time.
settings.s10: Comms rooms fail for physical reasons
settings.s11: Heat, dust and improvisation account for a large share of hardware failures. A rack in a cupboard with no ventilation will shorten the life of everything in it, and a rack with no patching discipline turns a five-minute change into an afternoon. Ventilation, power, containment and labelling are not tidiness for its own sake; they decide how long a fault takes to find.
settings.s13: Labelling and records are the part that gets skipped
settings.s14: An unlabelled patch field means every future change begins with tracing. A documented schedule mapping outlet to patch panel to switch port turns that into a two-minute job. It is the cheapest thing to do during installation and the most expensive to reconstruct afterwards.

settings.s2: The disruptive part is access, not the cable
settings.s3: Most of the work in an occupied building is about getting to places: ceilings, risers, and rooms that can only be entered outside business hours. settings.s4: New sites and fit-outs are considerably cheaper to cable before fit-out finishes than after, so this is worth raising early in any move. Cabling underpins everything else on the network, particularly
